title: Sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:30–44)
hook: he looks at the crowd with compassion and feeds five thousand

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's head: a ruler's oath at a feast, and a good man killed for it. Your line was careless words cost lives. Which promise did you keep? Day one hundred eighty-three.

The twelve come back from their travels, full of stories, and exhausted. So many people are coming and going that they don't even have time to eat. Jesus says, come away with me to a quiet place and rest a while. They get in the boat. And the crowd sees where they're headed and runs around the shore on foot, and gets there first. The boat lands, and there they are. Thousands. The day off is gone before it starts. Mark tells us what Jesus felt. Today: sheep without a shepherd.
screen: `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `COME AWAY AND REST.` → `THE CROWD GETS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: Jesus "saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd." Moved with compassion is a gut word in Greek: the verb is about the insides, compassion felt deep in the body. And sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase in Israel's scriptures, for a people with no one to guide or protect them. So he teaches them many things, until the day is far spent. Then it's late, in the middle of nowhere, and the disciples do the sensible thing: send them away to buy food. And Jesus answers: "Give ye them to eat." You give them something. They do the math out loud: should they go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread? He asks, what have you got? Five loaves and two fish. He has everyone sit in groups on the grass. Mark notices it was green, which some read as a hint of spring. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Take, bless, break, give: Christian readers hear those same four actions again at the Last Supper, and at the communion table today. Everyone eats and is satisfied. And the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Some readers smile that there is one for each disciple who said send them away. About five thousand men, Mark says; Matthew adds, besides women and children. Christians have read it as a miracle of Jesus's power and a picture of God feeding his people. Some also notice what he did with the disciples: he didn't let them off the hook. He started with their little and put it in their hands.
screen: `MOVED WITH COMPASSION.` · `GIVE YE THEM TO EAT.` · `TAKE, BLESS, BREAK, GIVE.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see a crowd with compassion. Settle, and breathe. Picture a crowd you'll be part of today. A commute, a store, a feed full of strangers, a waiting room. A crowd can feel like an obstacle. Try seeing it the way the text says Jesus did. Faces that might be tired. Faces hungry for something. Some with no one looking out for them. Notice what stirs, if anything. If you pray, you can pray for that crowd. Then ask what little you have that could go into someone's hands. The bell holds the time.
Compassion, the gut-deep feeling, in Greek, behind Jesus seeing a tired crowd not as a nuisance but as sheep without a shepherd.
Your line: you give them something. Today, when you're tempted to send a need away, see what little you have and give it. Day one hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians connect the feeding of the five thousand with communion, where bread is blessed, broken and given, and churches often run food banks and shared meals with this story in mind.

what it means: Jesus feels gut-deep compassion for a leaderless crowd, and makes his disciples start with what little they have.
what a scholar hears: take, bless, break, give: the same four verbs as the Last Supper, and sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase from Israel's scriptures.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: 'Jesus says four words: Give ye them to eat' was a miscount (five words), now fixed; 'two hundred days' wages' replaced by the text's 'two hundred pennyworth'; cut 'only Mark says green', 'you know that week', 'most of us would sigh', 'for hours' and 'he felt it in his stomach'; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.
'Two hundred pennyworth' (200 denarii) glossed as 'two hundred days' wages'; confirm.
'Only Mark says green' — John 6:10 mentions 'much grass' but not green; Matthew 14:19 'grass'. Confirm the claim is precise enough.
Twelve baskets 'one for each disciple who said send them away' is an interpretive flourish, now attributed to 'some readers'; confirm.
Four verbs changed from look up/bless/break/give to take/bless/break/give: Mark 14:22 has took, blessed, brake, gave, and has no looking up. Mark 6:41 has all five. Confirm.
Mark 6:44 says only about five thousand men; the earlier line not counting everyone else was replaced with Matthew 14:21 besides women and children, credited to Matthew. Confirm.
Green grass pointing to spring was stated as settled; softened to may point to spring.
Sheep without a shepherd: Numbers 27:17; Ezekiel 34:5; 1 Kings 22:17. Confirm.
